title: The Year Christendom Split
teaser: In Rome and Avignon, two popes excommunicate each other. In Florence, wool carders seize the government. In Padua, Altichiero paints crowds at the cross. Everywhere, the old certainties crack.

art.label: Art
art.content: In Padua, Altichiero da Zevio completes his monumental Crucifixion fresco in the Chapel of San Giacomo at the Basilica di Sant'Antonio. The work represents the final flowering of Trecento naturalism — Giotto's revolution absorbed and extended. Altichiero fills his Crucifixion with over a hundred figures: Roman soldiers, grieving disciples, fainting women, indifferent bystanders. Contemporary portraits appear throughout — Petrarch's face haunts the crowd, King Louis I of Hungary appears in council scenes. The space is deep, the architecture convincing, the emotion individualized. This is painting on the cusp: still Gothic in its gold grounds and pointed arches, already proto-Renaissance in its psychological realism. Altichiero's patrons, the Lupi di Soragna family, commissioned the chapel as a statement of dynastic power in turbulent times.

lit.label: Literature
lit.content: In England, William Langland is revising his allegorical masterpiece Piers Plowman — the B-text, composed between 1377 and 1379, transforms his visionary poem into a searing critique of late medieval society. Written in alliterative Middle English, it follows the dreamer Will through corrupted fields, plowmen who cannot find truth, and a Church that has lost its way. Langland writes for common readers in their own tongue. Meanwhile, Catherine of Siena — mystic, diplomat, future Doctor of the Church — has just completed her Dialogue of Divine Providence, dictated in ecstatic visions between 1377 and 1378. She writes in Tuscan vernacular, not Latin, insisting that God speaks through laypeople too. Two vernaculars, two visions, both demanding reform.

phil.label: Philosophy
phil.content: Catherine of Siena embodies a new kind of philosophical authority: the mystical theologian who bypasses clerical mediation to claim direct conversation with God. Her Dialogue presents Christ as a bridge between human and divine — but the bridge is accessible to anyone who seeks it, not controlled by institutional gatekeepers. In England, John Wycliffe pushes this logic further. His De civili dominio (1376-1378) argues that a Church fallen into sin has no right to property, that Scripture alone holds authority, that the papacy itself lacks biblical warrant. Pope Gregory XI condemns nineteen of Wycliffe's propositions in 1377, but powerful nobles protect him. The philosophical ground is shifting: nominalism has severed universals from particulars, and now authority itself seems unmoored from any stable foundation.

hist.label: History
hist.content: On 8 April 1378, a Roman mob surrounds the papal conclave, demanding an Italian pope. The cardinals, terrified, elect Bartolomeo Prignano as Urban VI. Within months, his abrasive reformism alienates the French cardinals. On 20 September 1378, they meet at Fondi and elect Robert of Geneva as Clement VII, who establishes his court at Avignon. The Western Schism begins: two popes, each excommunicating the other's followers, Europe splitting along political lines. In Florence that July, something equally unprecedented: the Ciompi Revolt. Wool carders and unskilled laborers — the popolo minuto without guild representation — storm the Palazzo Vecchio. Michele di Lando, a wool carder, becomes Gonfaloniere of Justice. Three new guilds are created. For six weeks, Florence has a workers' government.

conn.label: Connections
conn.content: The threads converge in a single question: who holds legitimate authority? In Rome, the cardinals say their first election was coerced — authority requires free consent. In Avignon, Clement VII says the office matters more than the man. Catherine of Siena rushes to Rome to defend Urban VI, writing furious letters calling Clement's cardinals 'incarnate demons'. Wycliffe uses the schism to argue that the papacy itself is illegitimate. In Florence, the Ciompi ask why only guildsmen can govern — why not those who actually work the wool? Altichiero's Crucifixion shows us the other side of crisis: a crowd at the foot of the cross, each face distinct, each responding differently to the same event. There is no single authorized reaction. The center cannot hold because people have stopped believing it was ever the center.
conn.funFact: Catherine of Siena couldn't write until age thirty. She dictated her Dialogue to secretaries while in ecstatic trances, eyes fixed on nothing visible, speaking as if taking God's dictation.
